title: Weilüe (魏略), 'Peoples of the West' — Section 11, The Kingdom of Da Qin (Rome)
language_note: Classical Chinese. The Weilüe itself is lost as an independent work; this section survives because Pei Songzhi quoted it in his 429 CE commentary to the Sanguozhi (Wei Shu 30). Original composed by Yu Huan, c. 239-265 CE.
date: composed c. 239-265 CE; describes conditions as of the early 3rd century CE
original_text_excerpt: 大秦國一號犁靬，在安息、條支西大海之西，從安息界安穀城乘船，直截海西，遇風利二月到，風遲或一歲，無風或三歲。其國在海西，故俗謂之海西。有河出其國，西又有大海。海西有遲散城，從國下直北至烏丹城，西南又渡一河，乘船一日乃過。西南又渡一河，一日乃過。凡有大都三，卻從安穀城陸道直北行之海北，復直西行之海西，復直南行經之烏遲散城，渡一河，乘船一日乃過。周回繞海，凡當渡大海六日乃到其國。國有小城邑合四百餘，東西南北數千里。其王治濱側河海，以石爲城郭。
original_text_note: Verbatim Classical Chinese recovered 2026-08-22 from the Chinese Wikisource transcription of 三國志/卷30 (Sanguozhi, Wei Shu 30), where Pei Songzhi's 429 CE commentary quotes the Weilüe's 西戎傳. 221 characters, contiguous, running from 大秦國一號犁靬 to 以石爲城郭。 NOTHING WAS STRIPPED: the span sits inside a single paragraph and carries no line breaks, no editorial brackets and no wiki-link markup. The underlying text is a third-century work long in the public domain; the Wikisource transcription is CC BY-SA 4.0. CITATION CORRECTED IN THE SAME PASS. citation_original previously named the Chinese Wikisource '魏略輯本' page, which does NOT contain this text: that edition's index lists 西戎傳 — including 大秦國 — under 卷二十二, and 卷二十二 is an unwritten page. The text was never obtainable from the cited source, which is the likeliest explanation for what was in this field before. WHAT WAS IN THIS FIELD BEFORE WAS NOT A PARAPHRASE AND NOT AN EXCERPT. It was 52 characters of plausible Classical Chinese that do not occur in the Weilüe. Checked fragment by fragment against the source: all three of its fragments are ABSENT, 0 of 3. Four divergences, and in each the old form appears nowhere in the source while the real form is present — 犂靬 for 犁靬 (the name Lijian), 安谷城 for 安穀城 (the city Angu), 城以石為壁 for 以石爲城郭 (the stone walls), 海西人名之海西 for 故俗謂之海西 ('called Haixi'). ingest.fidelity classified it `partial_verbatim`, eligible for retrieval; it has no way to detect this. Across the 15 archived runs of the chinese-da-qin gold case, 40 of 40 resolved quotations came from reference_translation and none from this field — the answer path had been routing around it for the whole of Part 7 and Part 8 without anyone knowing why. WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT TAKEN. The Da Qin section continues past this span (其土地有松、柏… through the products, the kingship, the dependencies, to 所傳聞西之極矣。). The span ends exactly where reference_translation ends, so the original and the translation cover the same ground and neither claims more than the other. Extending both is a Block F decision, not an ingestion one.
reference_translation: The kingdom of Da Qin (Rome) is also called Lijian. It is west of Anxi (Parthia) and Tiaozhi (Characene and Susiana), and west of the Great Sea. From the city of Angu (Gerrha), on the frontier of Anxi (Parthia), you take a boat and cut directly across to Haixi ('West of the Sea' = Egypt). With favourable winds it takes two months; if the winds are slow, perhaps a year; if there is no wind, perhaps three years... This country (the Roman Empire) has more than four hundred smaller cities and towns. It extends several thousand li in all directions. The king has his capital (that is, the city of Rome) close to the mouth of a river (the Tiber). The outer walls of the city are made of stone.
translation_source: John E. Hill, 'The Peoples of the West from the Weilüe by Yu Huan: A Third Century Chinese Account Composed between 239 and 265 CE', draft annotated translation, University of Washington Silk Road Seattle project.
notes: This is the exact hero-demo source named in the project's AI Technology Showcase brief ('Retrieves the Weilue passage on Da Qin in Classical Chinese'). High priority for the cross-lingual retrieval sanity check — pair with the Hou Hanshu 166 CE envoy passage (eastasia-02) for a same-topic, two-source comparison.

subject_places.name: Da Qin
subject_places.note: 大秦, the passage's subject — the Roman Empire, also called 犁靬 Lijian in the same sentence. A polity, not a settlement, and Pleiades holds no entry for it under any form searched. The English gloss identifies it with Rome, but that is the translator's identification and the record carries no citation for it, so the honest ground is regional with no id rather than `identified` without the scholar who made the identification. Pleiades 423025 Roma 41.890/12.491 was examined and is not used: the city is not the empire, and the ruling stands on that ground alone. A second reason given here on 2026-08-13 — that the Chinese excerpt was elided at exactly the point where the capital is described — is SUPERSEDED as of 2026-08-22: the verbatim text now in original_text_excerpt reads 其王治濱側河海，以石爲城郭, so the capital IS described. The elision was an artefact of a fabricated excerpt, not a property of the source. The decision is unchanged; one of its two reasons is withdrawn.

subject_places.name: Anxi
subject_places.note: 安息, west of which Da Qin lies — Parthia. Refused: 952097 'Parthyene/Parthia' 38.500/57.500 and 590282460 'Parthian empire', which is locationPrecision 'related' and dated **2000..2099** — a modern label, not an ancient place. Both are identifications of the Chinese name rather than the name itself, and the record has no citation for either.

subject_places.name: Tiaozhi
subject_places.note: 條支, named beside Anxi. UPGRADED FROM 'regional' 2026-08-13. A4 examined Pleiades 912905 and refused it with one stated reason — ‘it is the gloss’s identification and no citation supports it here’ — and that reason, and only that one, is now met by Paolillo 2024. This is a territory-to-territory identification, so it does not repeat the objection that sank Da Qin (the city of Rome is not the empire) or the one that sank Haixi (in the Weilüe, 海西 is an epithet of Da Qin, not a separate country). Confirmed against the Pleiades places snapshot of 2026-08-10 by coordinate — 31.468, 47.344 — title ‘Mesene/Characene/Shad Bahman/Maisan’, locationPrecision ‘precise’, attested -30..640, which overlaps this project’s -27..1204. NOTE THE NEAR MISS: the same snapshot holds 897810, also titled ‘Mesene’, a settlement near Ctesiphon whose ‘location has not been determined’. It is a different place and carries no coordinate; 912905 is the kingdom this identification is about. NOT marked contested: the scholarship varies over the extent rather than the referent — Hill glosses ‘Characene and Susiana’, Paolillo has Characene/Mesene ‘or its political centre Charax Spasinou’ — and flagging that as contested would dilute a flag that currently means a genuine two-sided dispute over which place is meant.
subject_places.ground_citation: Maurizio Paolillo, 'Following a Mediterranean Clue. A Reconsideration of the Sources About the Country of Haixi 海西國 (2nd-3rd Cent. CE)', in Renata Vinci (ed.), Navigating the Mediterranean Through the Chinese Lens: Transcultural Narratives of the Sea Among Lands, Firenze University Press, 2024, pp. 25-37, at p. 30: “Tiaozhi, on the other hand, appears to correspond with the territory of Characene/Mesene in southern Mesopotamia or its political centre Charax Spasinou”. Peer-reviewed, open access under CC BY 4.0. DOI 10.36253/979-12-215-0598-6.04

subject_places.name: Angu
subject_places.note: 安穀城, the city on the Parthian frontier (spelled 安谷城 here until 2026-08-22, a form absent from the source) where one takes ship. The gloss offers Gerrha; Pleiades holds no resolving entry for it, only the name 'sinus Gerrhaicus' on 932455, which is a gulf and not the city.

subject_places.name: Haixi
subject_places.note: 海西, 'west of the sea', where the crossing lands. The gloss identifies it with Egypt; that identification is the translator's and is not cited, so Pleiades 766 Aegyptus is deliberately NOT used here even though it is used for Egypt elsewhere in this corpus — there the Greek names Αἴγυπτος outright, and here the text names 海西.
